title: Who Will Be My Guarantor?
summary: Job continues his reply to Eliphaz. His spirit is broken, the grave is waiting, and mockers surround him. He asks God himself to put up the pledge for him, since no one else will, and describes how he has become a byword that people spit at. Yet he insists that the righteous hold to their way. He ends by asking where his hope is, and whether it will go down with him into the dust of Sheol.
story: Chapter 16 rose to Job's declaration that his witness is in heaven. Chapter 17 finishes the same speech, and it sinks again. This rise and fall is typical of Job's speeches in the middle of the book: a moment of daring hope is followed by exhaustion and gloom. Yet the thread of hope is not cut. In verse 3 Job asks God to stand surety for him, extending the idea of the heavenly witness. The chapter's closing questions about hope lead into Bildad's second speech (chapter 18), which answers with a grim portrait of the wicked, and then into Job's great reply in chapter 19.
historical:
The chapter's central image in verse 3 comes from ancient commercial and legal practice. When someone took on a debt or obligation, another person could stand as guarantor, promising to pay or answer if the first failed. The arrangement was sealed publicly, often by striking hands. The book of Proverbs repeatedly warns against rashly becoming surety for a neighbor or stranger (Proverbs 6:1-5; 17:18; 22:26), which shows how common and how risky the practice was. Judah offered himself as surety for Benjamin to his father Jacob (Genesis 43:9), taking on his brother's fate as his own.

Job applies this to his case with God. No human will stand as guarantor for him; his friends have abandoned him. So he asks God to lay down the pledge and to guarantee Job's case before God. It is the same paradox as chapter 16: Job appeals to God to be on his side against the charges he feels God is bringing.
cultural:
Two public forms of shame in the chapter would have struck an ancient reader hard. A byword (verse 6) was a name that became proverbial, used in taunts and sayings as an example of disaster. Israel's covenant curses warned that a disobedient people would become a byword among the nations (Deuteronomy 28:37), so being made one was a sign, in popular thinking, of divine punishment. Spitting in someone's face was a gesture of extreme contempt, used in the law as a public rebuke (Deuteronomy 25:9) and seen as disgrace (Numbers 12:14).

Verse 14 draws on family language to describe death. Calling corruption (or the pit, as some translations render the word) my father and the worm my mother or sister means treating decay as one's closest kin, the household one is about to join. For a man whose children are dead and whose relatives have turned away (as chapter 19 will describe), the image is desolate: the only family left to welcome him is the grave.
literary: The chapter is uneven and sometimes hard to follow in Hebrew, and several verses (especially 5 and 12) are obscure. Its movement is still clear. Verses 1-2 lament Job's broken spirit and his mockers. Verses 3-5 appeal to God for a pledge and condemn the friends. Verses 6-9 describe Job's public shame, and verses 8-9 surprisingly assert that upright people will be appalled and the righteous will hold to their way, a thought that seems to steady Job himself. Verse 10 challenges the friends to try again. Verses 11-16 close with a funeral meditation: Sheol as home, a bed spread in darkness, corruption as father, and the double question of verse 15 about where hope can be found. The chapter ends with a question, not an answer, and the question is about hope.

outline.t: Lay down a pledge for me
A byword, yet the righteous hold their way

doctrines.note: The chapter asks where hope can be found when everything visible points to the grave. Job's question is not answered here, but the fact that he keeps asking, and keeps asking God, is itself a form of hope.
Verse 9 says the righteous hold to their way and grow stronger. In the middle of his despair Job affirms that faithfulness is worth keeping, even when it brings no visible reward.
Job suffers not only in body but in reputation, becoming a byword and an object of spitting. The Bible recognizes public shame as a real and deep form of suffering.

words.note: Arav, to pledge or to stand surety, to take responsibility for another's debt. In verse 3 Job asks God to provide the pledge that God himself requires. The same verb is used of Judah offering himself for Benjamin (Genesis 43:9) and of the risky suretyship Proverbs warns against.

Taqa, to blow a trumpet, drive a peg, or strike hands. In verse 3 it refers to striking hands to seal a pledge, the ancient handshake that made a guarantee binding. Job asks who else will strike hands with him.

Meshol, a byword, a name that becomes proverbial for disaster. In verse 6 Job says God has made him a byword among the people, which means his name has become a standing example of divine judgment in popular talk.
Tiqvah, hope, used twice in verse 15. The question where then is my hope? gathers up the whole chapter, and it echoes chapter 14, where Job said God destroys a man's hope.

christ: Job's request that God himself would be his guarantor (verse 3) finds a striking echo in the New Testament. Hebrews says that Jesus has become the guarantor of a better covenant (Hebrews 7:22), using the same legal idea: one who stands surety and takes responsibility for another's obligations. Christians confess that in Christ God himself did what Job asked, providing the pledge that he requires and answering for those who could not answer for themselves. Job's description of being spat upon and made a byword also resonates with the Gospels' account of Jesus, who was mocked and spat upon (Mark 15:19). These are thematic connections, not predictions in Job's words, but they show how Job's cry points toward the gospel's answer.

hard.q: Has Job given up hope by the end of this chapter?
hard.a: The chapter ends darkly. Job speaks of the grave as his home, corruption as his father, and asks, “where then is my hope? Who can see any hope for me?” Some readers take this as the low point of Job's faith, a moment when he no longer expects anything from God. Others point out that the chapter contains signs of hope that have not disappeared. In verse 3 Job still appeals to God to be his guarantor, and in verse 9 he affirms that the righteous hold to their way and grow stronger. His questions are asked of God and before God, not in abandonment of him. A common reading is that Job has lost hope in anything he can see, including recovery in this life, but has not stopped reaching toward God. That reading is supported by chapter 19, where the same man declares that his Redeemer lives. A reader who finds Job's words about the grave matching their own sense that hope is gone should not wait out that darkness alone; a trusted friend, a pastor, a doctor, or a crisis line can help right now.

questions: Job asks God to be his guarantor when no one else will stand with him. When have you felt that no one would vouch for you, and where did you look for help?
Job says the righteous hold to their way even when it brings no reward. What helps you keep faith when faithfulness seems to cost more than it gives?
Job asks, where then is my hope? How would you answer a friend who asked you that question honestly?
